## Abstract

Rab GTPases play an essential role in the regulation of intracellular transport including the budding, tethering, and fusion of vesicles as well as organelle motility. The regulation of G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) trafficking by Rab GTPases has traditionally been regarded as a non-specific process that facilitates the movement of the receptors between intracellular membrane compartments. Thus, alterations in GPCR signal transduction and trafficking following the overexpression of constitutively active and dominant negative Rabs were originally considered to be solely the passive by-product of perturbations in intracellular compartmental dynamics. Recently, an explosion of experimental studies has provided increasingly convincing evidence that receptor trafficking actively affects the signal transduction of cargo proteins and that the signaling of GPCR vesicular cargo can in turn modulate Rab GTPase regulated intracellular transport processes. This research is revealing how different Rabs coordinate with themselves and other regulatory molecules to mediate protein trafficking, as well as uncovers novel functions for traditional Rabs, while illustrating the active role these trafficking molecules play in pathology of disease. Recently published in the Journal of Neuroscience, Esseltine et al., present a novel role for the typified exocytic small G protein Rab8 in the intracellular trafficking and signal transduction of metabotropic glutamate receptor 1.

**Keywords:** G protein-coupled receptors, Rab GTPase, desensitization, endocytosis, glutamate, signaling, trafficking

## Role for Rab GTPases in the Regulation of GPCR Activity

Agonist-activation of signal transduction cascades through G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) comprises both G protein-dependent and -independent signaling resulting in the activation of parallel signaling cascades and complex signaling networks.[1](#R1) Because cells express hundreds of different receptors, a mechanism to organize signal cascades must be put in place. One major mechanism of spatiotemporal signal organization includes protein intracellular trafficking.[2](#R2) In addition to contributing to the rapid and effective desensitization of GPCR signaling, the endocytosis and intracellular trafficking of GPCRs can spatially and temporally determine G protein-dependent and -independent signaling pathways. Membrane trafficking may also provide novel compartments for signal transduction. Receptors, such as the β2\-adrenergic receptor (β2AR), which recycle quickly and efficiently, also resensitize following either persistent or repeated agonist activation, whereas receptors, such as angiotensin type 1 receptor (AT1R), are retained in early endosomes and remain desensitized for longer periods of time.[3](#R3) However, receptor trafficking can be much more complex, as β2AR recycling has also been shown to actually switch the receptor’s traditional coupling with Gαs to Gαi, and the AT1R compartmentalizes extracellular regulated kinase (ERK1/2) complexes to endosomes.[1](#R1),[4](#R4)

Less well understood are the direct and indirect roles of GPCR signal transduction on the regulation of the trafficking machinery itself, although it is now proposed that receptors participate in the modulation of their own intracellular trafficking.[5](#R5),[6](#R6) For example, AT1R activation causes GDP for GTP exchange on Rab5a resulting in Rab5 activation and homotypic endosomal vesicular fusion, while p38 MAPK activation stimulates the formation of Rab5-guanine dissociation inhibitor (GDI) complexes, thereby increasing endocytosis.[5](#R5),[7](#R7) PKA activation by the β2AR regulates Rab4, but not Rab11 recycling pathways, and β2AR also modulates the geranyl-geranylation of both Rab11 and Rab8, altering the ability of these Rabs to associate with membranes, and thus modifying their overall functional activity.[8](#R8),[9](#R9) Rab GTPases have been shown to bind to a number of additional GPCRs including the α2BAR, thromboxane A2 receptor, prostacyclin receptor and metabotropic glutamate receptor 1a (mGluR1a).[5](#R5),[10](#R10)\-[14](#R14) The association of Rab GTPases with GPCRs is mediated by specific amino acid residues within the carboxyl-terminal tails of GPCRs that do not conform to a conserved consensus sequence. Rab binding to the AT1R C-tail is mediated by proline residue 354 and cysteine residue 355, and Rab4, Rab5, Rab7 and Rab11 each compete for the same binding site.[15](#R15) The functional consequence of these competitive interactions determines whether the AT1R is retained in the early endosomal compartment, is dephosphorylated and recycled back to the plasma or is targeted to late endosomes for lysosomal degradation.[15](#R15),[16](#R16) In contrast, Rab 11 binding to the thromboxane A2 receptor C-tail is mediated by amino acid residues 335–345, whereas Rab11 binding to the β2AR C-tail is mediated a bipartite binding motif, with arginine 333 and lysine 348 representing the essential amino acid residues mediating Rab11 binding to the receptor.[10](#R10),[11](#R11) The precise localization of Rab8 interactions with the mGluR1a C-tail has yet to be determined, but Rab8 does not regulate the activity of the mGluR1b alternative splice variant lacking an extended carboxyl-terminal tail.[14](#R14)

## Rab8 Regulation of GPCR Activity

Rab8 is enriched in the brain, is localized to Golgi, vesicles and membrane ruffles, is involved in trafficking of basolateral proteins in polarized epithelial cells and plays a role in neurite outgrowth.[17](#R17) Rab8 is also documented in the polarized transport of rhodopsin in photoreceptor cells and is found in the primary cilia of the cell.[18](#R18)\-[20](#R20) Rab8 also directly associates with the α2B\- and β2\-adrenergic receptors, and a GDP-bound dominant negative Rab8 mutant blocks α2BAR cell surface expression and ERK1/2 activation, but has no effect on β2AR localization and signaling.[12](#R12) In a recent report, Esseltine and coworkers[14](#R14) have demonstrated that Rab8 also interacts in an agonist regulated manner with the long carboxyl-terminal tail of the mGluR1a, but not mGluR1b splice variant. As a consequence, the association of Rab8 with mGluR1a selectively regulates mGluR1a endocytosis and signaling. Specifically, Rab8 functions to attenuate both mGluR1a internalization and inositol phosphate signaling in human embryonic kidney (HEK 293) cells and Ca2+ signaling in primary hippocampal neurons. Thus, contrary to other reports, which indicate that Rab8 expression facilitates receptor signaling by increased cell surface expression, Rab8-mediated increases in mGluR1a plasma membrane expression resulted in decreased receptor signaling both in HEK 293 cells and hippocampal neurons.

The attenuation of mGluR1a-stimulated inositol phosphate formation following Rab8 overexpression is reversed by the treatment of HEK 293 cells with the protein kinase C (PKC) inhibitors bisindolylmaleimide-1 and chelerythrine chloride.[14](#R14) This suggests the Rab8 mediated attenuation of mGluR1a endocytosis may serve to increase second messenger-dependent kinase-mediated phosphorylation and desensitization by preventing mGluR1a dephosphorylation. The dephosphorylation of GPCRs, such as the β2AR, is dependent upon agonist-stimulated receptor endocytosis to the endosomal compartment where the β2AR is dephosphorylated as it transits from the Rab5 positive early endosomal compartment to the Rab4 positive recycling endosomal compartment.[21](#R21) Although dephosphorylation of cAMP-dependent protein kinase phosphorylated β2AR does not require endocytosis,[22](#R22) it remains unknown whether the dephosphorylation of PKC phosphorylated mGluR1a either occurs at the cell surface or requires endocytosis to endosomes. Thus, we hypothesize that mGluR1a dephosphorylation does not occur at the cell surface, and Rab8-dependent cell surface mGluR1a retention prevents the dephosphorylation of PKC phosphorylated mGluR1a in the endosomal compartment. The extent of mGluR1a endocytosis in a given cell type is likely not regulated by Rab8 alone, but also involves a dynamically balanced association with other proteins that regulate the constitutive and agonist-stimulated internalization of mGluR1a, such as G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2, phospholipase D and Ral A.[23](#R23)\-[26](#R26) Future investigation will be required to determine the functional dynamics underlying the overall regulation of mGluR1a endocytosis and its relative role in regulating the desensitization and resensitization of mGluR1a responsiveness.

Multiple Rabs have been shown to be involved in the regulation of both endocytosis and recycling of GPCRs.[5](#R5),[10](#R10)\-[14](#R14) However, to our knowledge, Rab8 represents the first example of a Rab GTPase that functions to attenuate the endocytosis and trafficking of a GPCR, thereby providing an additional avenue by which Rabs regulate GPCR activity and localization. One consequence of blocking mGluR1a internalization in HEK 293 cells is to increase the cell surface localization of the receptor. While this increase in cell surface expression did not have an overall effect on mGluR1a signaling in an overexpression system (HEK 293 cells) or Ca2+ signaling in neurons, it is unknown whether this might increase the localization of mGluR1a expression at the post-synaptic membrane in neurons to modulate the efficacy of synaptic transmission. For example, it has previously been demonstrated that Rab8 plays an important role in regulating the synaptic delivery of AMPA receptors during long-term potentiation and during constitutive receptor recycling.[27](#R27),[28](#R28) Thus, it is reasonable to hypothesize that Rab8 may also regulate the localization and insertion of mGluR1a into the post synaptic density as an adaptive response increased synaptic activity.

## Role of Rab Proteins in Huntington Disease

Huntington disease is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by an abnormal polyglutamine expansion in the N-terminus of the huntingtin (Hdh) protein, leading to cell dysfunction and neuronal death.[29](#R29),[30](#R30) As is found for Rab8-mediated desensitization of mGluR1a signaling, the attenuation of mGluR5 signaling observed in HdhQ111/Q111 mice is also PKC-dependent.[31](#R31) This PKC-dependent attenuation of mGluR5 signaling is neuroprotective, as PKC inhibitor treatment of neurons derived from HdhQ111/Q111 mice that are treated with the mGluR1/5 selective agonist DHPG exhibit increased DHPG-mediated cell death when compared with control neurons. However, neurons derived from HdhQ111/Q111 mice that lack mGluR5 expression (HdhQ111/Q111 mice crossed with mGluR5 knockout mice) are resistant to the neurotoxic effects of the combined treatment with DHPG and a PKC inhibitor.

The Rab8 effector protein, optineurin, also interacts with both mGluR1a and poly-glutamine expanded mutant huntingtin protein to antagonize mGluR1a-stimulated inositol phosphate formation.[32](#R32) Optineurin colocalizes with huntingtin in the Golgi apparatus, where it participates with Rab8 to coordinate post-Golgi protein transport.[33](#R33) However, whether Rab8 also contributes to the post-Golgi transport of mGluR1a/5 and whether this is altered in mutant huntingtin mouse model remains to be determined. Another Rab GTPase, Rab11, likely also contributes to the pathology of Huntington disease. In particular, Rab11-dependent vesicle formation is impaired in fibroblasts derived in Huntington disease patients, and Rab11 dominant negative protein expressing adult mouse brains display a similar neurodegenerative phenotype to huntingtin mutant mouse models of Huntington disease.[34](#R34),[35](#R35) Both Rab 8 and Rab11 associate with the actin motor protein myosin Vb to regulate trafficking.[36](#R36) Therefore, it is possible that Rab8 and Rab11 work in concert to regulate mGluR1a/5 protein trafficking under normal conditions and that this is altered in Huntington disease. In summary, while it remains unknown what the relationship Rab8/optineurin interactions have to the pathophysiology of Huntington’s disease, our observations suggest a potential link between Rab8, optineurin and mutant huntingtin protein in the regulation of mGluR1/5 activity in Huntington disease.

## Key Points

-   Some of the clearest evidence on the localization of memory within the mammalian brain has come from studies of associative learning, especially through the use of classical or Pavlovian conditioning, in which animals learn to express a conditioned response to a predictive or conditioned stimulus (CS) paired with an unconditioned stimulus (US). This review focuses on two of the most widely used forms of Pavlovian learning: eyelid and fear conditioning.
    
-   In eyelid conditioning, the deep cerebellar nuclei and overlying cerebellar cortex seem to mediate the acquisition and storage of discrete motor memories. By contrast, evidence from fear conditioning points to the lateral nucleus of the amygdala (LA) as a key component of the brain system that is responsible for the formation of aversive emotional memories.
    
-   Despite being mediated by different brain systems, these forms of learning might use a similar sequence of events to form new memories. Recent data point to a 'trigger-and-storage' model, in which the initial encoding and subsequent long-term storage of memory are mediated by separate groups of neurons.
    
-   Two sets of cerebellar neurons, the Purkinje cells and neurons in the anterior interpositus nucleus, change their activity during eyelid conditioning and so represent potential sites of plasticity. Recent evidence indicates that the cerebellar cortex might participate in the initiation of learning, whereas the deep cerebellar nuclei are more involved in the long-term storage of memory.
    
-   The dorsal region of the LA (LAd) is a site of CS–US convergence. Two distinct sets of neurons in the LAd could contribute differentially to the initiation and storage of fear-conditioning memories. Cells in the dorsal tip of the LAd develop conditioning-induced enhancement of their auditory responses very early in training, but cells in more ventral regions take longer to reach maximal response levels.
    
-   Several important questions remain unanswered, including whether there is complete transfer of memory from the 'soft' trigger cells to the 'hard' storage cells. It is also not known whether plasticity in the trigger cells is required for the induction of plasticity in the storage cells, or if the induction of soft and hard plasticity can proceed independently, but at different rates.
    

## Abstract

Recent evidence from cerebellum-dependent motor learning and amygdala-dependent fear conditioning indicates that, despite being mediated by different brain systems, these forms of learning might use a similar sequence of events to form new memories. In each case, learning seems to induce changes in two different groups of neurons. Changes in the first class of cells are induced very rapidly during the initial stages of learning, whereas changes in the second class of cells develop more slowly and are resistant to extinction. So, anatomically distinct cell populations might contribute differentially to the initial encoding and the long-term storage of memory in these two systems.

# Mechanistic insights into Angelman's syndrome

-   [Cristian Bodo](#auth-Cristian-Bodo) 

[*Nature Reviews Neuroscience*](/nrn) **volume 11**, pages 298–299 (2010) [Cite this article](#citeas)

The authors showed that both membrane depolarization and glutamate receptor activation increased the levels of UBE3A mRNA and protein in cultured neurons and in the brains of mice housed in an enriched environment. Binding sites for myocyte enhancer factor 2, an activity-regulated transcription factor that controls synapse development, were found in the promoter region of the *Ube3a* gene. Using a transgenic mouse model expressing a haemagglutinin epitope-tagged version of ubiquitin, the authors identified candidate substrates of UBE3A in neurons. These candidates shared a region of similarity 75 amino-acids in length that could serve as a UBE3A-binding domain.

A search for sequence similarities in mammalian genome databases identified the synaptic protein ARC as a potential UBE3A substrate. ARC regulates AMPAR trafficking, providing a possible link with the role of UBE3A in synaptic function. To test whether UBE3A influences ARC levels, the authors co-expressed UBE3A and ARC *in vitro* and observed a decrease in the level of ARC that was prevented by the addition of a proteasome inhibitor to the culture medium. Moreover, ARC protein levels were increased in the brains of UBE3A-knockout mice. Blocking UBE3A expression in hippocampal neurons using RNA interference (RNAi) or by knocking out UBE3A *in vivo* decreased AMPAR levels at the plasma membrane and impaired AMPAR recruitment to the postsynaptic region. Furthermore, inhibition of UBE3A expression led to a reduction in the frequency (but not the amplitude) of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents, an effect that was attributed to the elimination of AMPAR expression from a subset of synapses. These changes were dependent on ARC ubiquitylation and degradation, as overexpression of a version of ARC lacking the UBE3A-binding domain mimicked the effect of UBE3A expression blockade, and ARC-specific RNAi increased surface AMPAR expression.

## Abstract

Using *de novo* protein design, we incorporated a copper metal binding site within the three-helix bundle *α*3D (Walsh et al. *Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A.* 1999, 96, 5486–5491) to assess whether a cupredoxin center within an *α*\-helical domain could mimic the spectroscopic, structural, and redox features of native type-1 copper (CuT1) proteins. We aimed to determine whether a CuT1 center could be realized in a markedly different scaffold rather than the native *β*\-barrel fold and whether the characteristic short Cu–S bond (2.1–2.2 Å) and positive reduction potentials could be decoupled from the spectroscopic properties (*ε*600 nm = 5000 M−1 cm−1) of such centers. We incorporated 2HisCys(Met) residues in three distinct *α*3D designs designated core (CR), chelate (CH), and chelate-core (ChC). XAS analysis revealed a coordination environment similar to reduced CuT1 proteins, producing Cu–S(Cys) bonds ranging from 2.16 to 2.23 Å and Cu–N(His) bond distances of 1.92–1.99 Å. However, Cu(II) binding to the CR and CH constructs resulted in tetragonal type-2 copper-like species, displaying an intense absorption band between 380 and 400 nm (>1500 M−1 cm−1) and A∥ values of (150–185) × 10−4 cm−4. The ChC construct, which possesses a metal-binding site deeper in its helical bundle, yielded a CuT1-like brown copper species, with two absorption bands at 401 (4429 M−1 cm−1) and 499 (2020 M−1 cm−1) nm and an A∥ value ~30 × 10−4 cm−4 greater than its native counterparts. Electrochemical studies demonstrated reduction potentials of +360 to +460 mV (vs NHE), which are within the observed range for azurin and plastocyanin. These observations showed that the designed metal binding sites lacked the necessary rigidity to enforce the appropriate structural constraints for a Cu(II) chromophore (EPR and UV–vis); however, the Cu(I) structural environment and the high positive potential of CuT1 centers were recapitulated within the *α*\-helical bundle of *α*3D.

## INTRODUCTION

Electron transfer (ET) is the simplest chemical transformation in a redox reaction and serves a central role in numerous bioenergetic processes including photosynthesis and respiration.[1](#R1),[2](#R2) Found in bacteria, algae, plants, and animals, cupredoxins or type-1 copper centers (CuT1) are electron transfer proteins that have been extensively studied to understand this fundamental reaction.[3](#R3)–[6](#R6) The copper ion is encompassed in a Greek *β*\-barrel fold and coordinated to three equatorial ligands, formed by two N(His) and one S(Cys), as well as one or two more weakly bound axial ligands, such as S(Met) or O(Gln), to form a three- to five-coordinate copper complex. The canonical CuT1 proteins give rise to unique spectroscopic, structural, and redox properties.[7](#R7),[8](#R8) For example, plastocyanin and azurin display an LMCT transition at 600 nm (3000–6000 M−1 cm−1), a compressed EPR hyperfine coupling constant (*A*∥) (<70 × 10−4 cm−1), a short Cu–S(Cys) bond of 2.1–2.2 Å, and highly positive reduction potentials (E°) of +180 to +800 mV (vs NHE). Green copper centers stellacyanin and the CuT1 center in copper nitrite reductase are characterized as perturbed blue copper centers with an additional LMCT band at ~450 nm (3000–6000 M−1 cm−1). Nitrosocyanin, a red copper center, is a recent addition to the CuT1 family and possesses the most perturbed copper site, exhibiting an inverted absorption spectrum with a *λ*max at 390 nm (7000 M−1 cm−1), as well as a large *A*∥ (144 × 10−4 cm−1), a Cu(II)–S(Cys) bond that is elongated by ~0.1 Å, and a reduction potential of +84 mV.[56](#R56) This red copper center possesses the characteristics of a type-2 copper site (CuT2) or a “normal” copper center such as Cu(II)Cl4.[7](#R7)

Protein design has proven to be an effective strategy for examining the metal active sites of native metalloproteins.[9](#R9)–[12](#R12) This biologically relevant approach has two central design strategies: the first is protein redesign/reengineering,[9](#R9) and the second is *de novo* design.[10](#R10)–[12](#R12) The second strategy employs first-principles to design an original sequence that forms the proper hydrophobic, electrostatic, and hydrogen-bonding interactions and manifests into a well-defined fold. *De novo* protein design offers a methodology in modeling the active sites of native proteins in a simplified or unrelated fold. DeGrado and co-workers made a significant advancement in protein design with their creation of a native-like scaffold, *α*3D.[13](#R13) In contrast to previous *de novo* *α*\-helical designs, *α*3D is a single polypeptide chain of 73 amino acids that folds into an antiparallel three-helix bundle and contains every natural amino acid residue except cysteine ([Table 1](#T1)). We recently functionalized the *α*3D scaffold with a metal binding site to produce *α*3DIV[14](#R14) and *α*3DH3.[15](#R15) The first derivative, *α*3DIV, contains a 3Cys site found in native CuT1 proteins to investigate the metallobiochemistry of toxic heavy metals,[14](#R14) and the NMR structure of apo *α*3DIV was subsequently solved to investigate the perturbation on the overall fold of *α*3D as a consequence of incorporating a 3Cys site in place of 3Leu residues.[16](#R16) The second derivative, *α*3DH3, possesses a 3His site that coordinates transition metal ions and was shown to recapitulate the catalytic reaction performed by carbonic anhydrase.[15](#R15)

In this work, we report the design process and characterization of copper metallopeptides that makes available a mixed first coordination sphere environment by modeling the 2HisCys(Met) metal binding site of native CuT1 proteins ([Figure 1](#F1)) within the *α*3D scaffold. The preassembled fold of *α*3D offers facile incorporation of a mixed-ligand site within a *de novo* designed scaffold. Utilizing the structure of *α*3DIV[16](#R16) as a foundation, we designed three distinct constructs, designated as *α*3D-core (CR), -chelate (CH), and -chelate-core (ChC) ([Table 1](#T1)). Our goal was to assess if the physical properties (e.g., absorption *λ*max at 600 nm, compressed *A*∥, short Cu–S(Cys) bond, and *E*° value >180 mV) of a metal center that is naturally observed in a *β*\-barrel fold can be achieved in the antiparallel three-helix bundle fold of *α*3D. Ultimately, the lessons learned from this work will provide the foundation to study long-rate ET reactions within a *de novo* designed framework and develop bifunctional/bimetallic constructs that contain a catalytic and an ET center, such as in copper nitrite reductase.

## EXPERIMENTAL SECTION

### Peptide Expression and Purification

A pET15B recombinant DNA plasmid that contains the gene for each construct was transformed and expressed in *E. coli* BL21(DE3) competent cells (Life Technologies). The plasmid for constructs *α*3D-CR1, *α*3D-CH3, *α*3D-CH4, and *α*3D-ChC2 ([Table 1](#T1)) were purchased from Celtek Genes. The Ala77Cys derivative of each construct was prepared for electrochemical studies. A GeneArt site-directed mutagenesis system (Life Technologies) was used to mutate the codon for Ala77 to Cys within the pET15b vector. These proteins were overexpressed in self-inducing media for 18 h, pelleted, resuspended in 1.0 mM phosphate buffer saline solution containing 2.0 mM dithiothreitol, and lysed by sonication. Protein purifications were performed using previously described methods.[16](#R16) These *α*3D derivatives with a GSGA tail have a yield of 100–200 mg/L, which improved expression yields by 2 to 4 times compared to *α*3DIV. The molecular weight is determined by ESI-MS (collected on a Micromass LCT time-of-flight mass spectrometer), which corresponds to the protein after the deletion of the N-terminal methionine residue. Protein concentrations were determined by measuring the absorbance at 280 nm using a determined *ε* = 5650 cm−1 M−1 (Trp) or 8215 cm−1 M−1 (Trp and Tyr).

### Circular Dichroism (CD) Spectroscopy

CD spectra were collected on an AVIV 202 CD spectrometer at 25 °C using 1 cm path length quartz cuvettes. Samples contained 10 mM phosphate buffer and 5 *μ*M peptide and were prepared at pH 7.5. The mean residue ellipticities (\[*θ*\]) and percent folding were based on the presence of 55 helical residues, which were determined from the structure of *α*3DIV[16](#R16) and were calculated using previously reported procedures.[17](#R17),[18](#R18) Guanidine hydrochloride (GuaHCl) titrations were performed using a Microlab 500 series syringe-pump automatic titrator controlled by Aviv software. In a solution of 5 *μ*M peptide in 10 mM phosphate buffer at pH 7.5, GuaHCl was titrated to a concentration of 5.0 M while maintaining the protein concentration. The change in molar ellipticity upon titration was fitted to a two-state unfolding model.[19](#R19)

### Ultraviolet–Visible (UV–Vis) and Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) Spectroscopy

UV–vis spectra were recorded at room temperature on a Cary 100 Bio UV–vis spectrometer, using 1 cm path length anaerobic quartz cuvettes. X-band EPR spectra were collected on a Bruker EMX electron spin resonance spectrometer with a Varian liquid nitrogen cryostat at 77 K. A stock solution of standardized copper chloride was the source of Cu(II) ions. For the UV–vis experiments, 50 *μ*M Cu(II) was added to a 100 *μ*M apopeptide solution that contained 50 mM HEPES buffer solution. The pH of the apo solution was adjusted to 7.5. The spectrum was scanned from 800 to 300 nm every 2 min. EPR samples comprised 1 mM Cu(II)-peptide complex (at 1:2 Cu(II):peptide ratio), 50 mM HEPES solution, and 30% glycerol. Each sample was then flash frozen in liquid N2. To obtain Cu(II) EPR parameters, each spectrum was simulated on SpinCount.[20](#R20)

### 113Cd NMR Experiments

113Cadium(II) NMR experiments were performed on a Varian VNMRS 700 MHz equipped with a room-temperature triple resonance switchable probe and were collected at 25 °C. The reported chemical shifts are relative to the corresponding value of Cd(ClO4)2, 642 ppm, which is used as a zero point. The NMR parameters involved a spectral width of 96 000 Hz, 5.0 *μ*s 90° pulse, and 0.05 s acquisition time with no delay between scans. Each sample was prepared by adding a small aliquot of 113Cd(NO3)2 (95% isotopically enriched 113CdO purchased from Oak Ridge National Lab) to an apopeptide solution containing 15% D2O/H2O. The final solution yielded a ~1 mM 113Cd-peptide (with 20% excess peptide) complex, and the pH was adjusted to 8.5 with concentrated KOH. The 113Cd NMR spectra were processed with MestreNova (version 10.0.0–14381) using a back linear prediction method.

### Determination of Cu(I) Dissociation Constants

The Cu(I)-peptide dissociation constants were determined using a competitive binding assay with disodium bathocuproindisulfonate (BCS) as the competitive chelator, expressed by the chemical equation: Cu(I)Pep + 2BCS ⇄ Cu(I)BCS2 + Pep. Each sample contained 25 *μ*M Cu(I)-pep (at a 1:2 ratio of Cu:pep) and 50 mM HEPES buffer set to pH 7.5. A small aliquot of BCS was titrated into a sample solution and stirred for 12 min. The titration experiments were completed in triplicates. The formation of CuBCS2 was tracked at 483 nm (*ε* = 13 300 cm−1 M−1), which has a log *β*2 of 19.8.[21](#R21) The binding constants were determined by fitting Abs vs BCS concentration plots on Hyperquad 2006 to the equation expressed above.

### XAS Analysis

Samples for X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) contained 1.0–2.0 mM Cu(I)-peptide complex, 50 mM buffer, and 30% glycerol in a glovebox. Samples were loaded into lucite XAS sample cells, frozen by immersion in liquid N2, and stored at this temperature until data collection. Data were collected at the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL) on beamline 7-3 with a Si(220) double-crystal monochromator and a Rh-coated harmonic rejection mirror upstream of the monochromator with a 12 keV energy cutoff to reject harmonics. Data were measured in fluorescence mode using a high-count-rate Canberra 30-element Ge array detector, with maximum count rates held below 120 kHz per channel. A Ni filter was placed in front of the detector to reduce the elastic scatter peak, and Soller slits were used to reduce the Ni fluorescence. An Oxford Instruments liquid helium cryostat was used to keep the samples below 10 K during data collection. Data were collected using 10 eV steps in the pre-edge region (8700–8950 eV), 0.25 eV for the edge (8950–9010 eV) region, and *k* = 0.05 Å−1 increments for the extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) region to *k* = 13.5 Å−1. These collections had integration times of 1 s in the pre-edge and edge regions and 1–20 s (*k*3 weighted) in the EXAFS region for a total scan time of ~40 min. Energies were calibrated by assigning the lowest energy inflection point of a copper metal foil as 8980.3 eV, placed between the second (I1) and third (I2) ionization chamber. An initial *E*0 value of 8990 eV was used to convert data to *k* space, and the background was removed using a three-region cubic spline. Data from each detector channel were inspected for glitches before inclusion in the final average. For the XANES pre-edge, subtraction and normalization to McMaster[22](#R22) values were carried out using the program MBACK.[23](#R23)

Raw data were converted to EXAFS and fitted using the EXAFSPAK[24](#R24) suite of programs, with theoretical amplitude and phase parameters calculated using FEFF 9.[25](#R25) Each complex was fitted with four models: model 1, three-atom 1S2N(His) fit; model 2, four-atom 2S2N(His) fit; model 3, four-atom SS′2N(His) fit; and model 4, four-atom 1S1O2N(His) fit ([Supporting Information, Table 2](#SD1)). Imidazole outer-shell scattering from the His was modeled using phase and amplitude parameters calculated for an idealized rigid Cu(imid)4 structure. The imidazole Debye–Waller factors were defined by assuming that the *σ*2 value for each scattering path increased proportionally from those calculated by Bunker and Dimakis for an ordered imidazole.[26](#R26) Two metal–ligand distances (*R*Cu–S, *R*Cu–N) and the Debye–Waller factors for the Cu–S and Cu–N shells (*σ*2Cu–S, *σ*2Cu–N) were the only adjustable parameters for models 1–3; for model 4 RCu–O and *σ*2Cu–O were also varied. The threshold energy *E*0 was fixed at 0 eV for all fits.

### Electrochemistry

Cyclic voltammetry measurements were obtained on a Metrohm AUTOLAB potentiostat (PGSTAT 12). The electrochemical apparatus contained a gold (Au) disk working electrode (0.008 cm2), a platinum wire counter electrode, and an aqueous saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode (0.241 V + SCE = normal hydrogen electrode). The gold surface was polished with aqueous alumina slurries having decreasing particle sizes in the following order: 1–0.3–0.05 *μ*m. Subsequently, the Au electrodes were conditioned in an electrochemical cell (under Arg), which contained 0.5 M H2SO4, by scanning 20 times from −300 mV to +1500 mV (vs SCE) at 500 mV/s until the cyclic voltammograms (CVs) overlaid well to indicate a homogeneous surface. The working electrode was also conditioned in the experiment cell, which comprised 0.1 M phosphate buffer and 0.1 M Na2SO4, scanning 10 times from −300 mV to +600 mV at 50 and 100 mV/s. After each electrode had been polished and conditioned, 20–50 *μ*L of a 0.5 mM Cu(I)-peptide Ala77Cys solution was chemically adsorbed on the Au surface in an anaerobic environment for 1–2 h. CVs were collected at varying scan rates and at room temperature (~22 °C). Additional cyclic voltammetry experiments were performed on a BASi Epsilon potentiostat. A platinum wire counter, working Au (0.0201 cm2), and Ag/AgCl (3.0 M NaCl) (0.210 V + Ag/AgCl = NHE) reference electrode were used in this experiment. This Au electrode was polished and conditioned, and the CVs were obtained using a similar procedure to that described above.

## RESULTS

### Solution Stability of Designed Constructs

The CD spectra of the apoform of *α*3D-CR1, *α*3D-CH3, *α*3D-CH4, and *α*3D-ChC2 (at pH 7.5) were collected to examine the perturbation of the overall fold of *α*3D caused by the incorporation of 2HisCys residues. This analysis, as well as denaturation experiments, was not performed for *α*3D-CH1, *α*3D-CH2, and *α*3D-ChC1 (*vide infra*). As shown in [Figure 2A](#F2), each CD spectrum displays double minima bands with large negative molar ellipticity values \[Θ\] at 208 and 222 nm, illustrating a CD profile of a relatively well-folded *α*\-helical scaffold.[27](#R27) The \[Θ\] indicated that *α*3D-CR1, *α*3D-CH3, and *α*3D-CH4 are ~80% *α*\-helical at pH 7.5. The same analysis performed on *α*3D-ChC2, which buries the 2HisCys ligands deeper inside the bundle, revealed a protein that is ~35% less *α*\-helical. The helicity of *α*3D-ChC2 is reminiscent of the BABY[28](#R28) three-stranded coiled-coil peptide that has a similar helical length to *α*3D. Guanidine hydrochloride titration experiments ([Figure 2B](#F2)) were performed to determine the Gibbs free energy of unfolding (Δ*G*u), degree of cooperativity (*m*), and midpoint of the transition (*C*m). These values were derived from a fit to a two-state unfolding model ([Table 2](#T2)). The *m* and *C*m values have a range of 1.0–3.0 kcal mol−1 M−1 and 0.8–1.0 M, respectively. The Δ*G*u parameter spans from 1.0 to 3.0 kcal mol−1, with *α*3D-CH4 demonstrating the highest value (3.2 kcal mol−1). *α*3D-ChC2 generated a broad denaturation shape, which indicated unfolding through several intermediate states, and the fit did not produce reliable denaturation parameters. Moreover, the corresponding experiments were performed on the Cu(I) adducts of each peptide to determine if metal binding improves stability. With the exception of Cu(I)*α*3D-CH3, which showed a ~ 15% decrease, Cu(I) binding did not affect the *α*\-helicity of these *α*3D derivatives. Excluding *α*3D-ChC2, the CD results showed that the apoforms have a high *α*\-helical content, which was the goal of *α*3D. Metal binding to the C-terminal end of the bundle (of *α*3D-CR1, *α*3D-CH3, and *α*3D-CH4) was not expected to necessarily increase the helicity of the peptide because the overall fold is intrinsically highly helical. It is expected that metal binding could perturb the environment around the metal binding site of the peptide. The Δ*G*u of Cu(I)*α*3D-CH3 increased by 0.7 kcal mol−1, while the corresponding parameter for Cu(I)*α*3D-CH4 decreased by 0.8 kcal mol−1 compared to its apo counterpart. These results could be ascertained by the position of its Cys residue compared to *α*3D-CH3. *α*3D-CH4 has a Cys residue at the 18th position, whereas *α*3D-CH3 contains the equivalent residue at position 21. The denaturation result of apo *α*3D-CH4 suggests that the permutation of the Cys residue to the 18th from the 21st position and *vice versa* for the His residue (18th to the 21st) improves the overall fold of the *α*3D-chelate construct by removing a bulky His and replacing it with a smaller Cys residue. Cu(I) binding to *α*3D-CH4 perturbs the environment near its metal binding site, lowering its stability, whereas Cu(I) bound to *α*3D-CH3 improves its stability at the cost of losing helicity. Additionally, Cu(I) binding to *α*3D-CR1 did not have a significant effect on its stability, whereas the fit on the denaturation curve of Cu(I)*α*3D-ChC2 generated CD parameters, indicating improvement on its stability when coordinated to Cu(I). The CD spectra and denaturation plots of the Cu(I) adducts are found in [Supporting Information, Figure 1](#SD1).

### Characterization of Cu(II) Complexes

UV–vis spectra were collected for the Cu(II) complex of *α*3D-CR1, *α*3D-CH3, *α*3D-CH4, and *α*3D-ChC2 ([Figure 3A](#F3)). These results are summarized in [Table 3](#T3) and compared to the corresponding properties of native and mutant CuT1 proteins, as well as CuT1 models in [Supporting Information, Table 1](#SD1). Cu(II)*α*3D-CR1 displayed a CuT2 species with an LMCT absorption band at 380 nm (1565 M−1 cm−1), a shoulder at 550 nm (438 M−1 cm−1), and a broad d–d-like band between 600 and 800 nm (300 M−1 cm−1). Cu(II)*α*3D-CH3 formed a yellow copper species with an intense band at 400 nm (2619 M−1 cm−1) and a broad band between 600 and 800 nm (300 M−1 cm−1). Similarly, the Cu(II) adduct of *α*3D-CH4 showed a *λ*max at 377 nm (1840 M−1 cm−1). This complex, however, has additional red-shifted bands at 450 (1098 M−1 cm−1) and 520 (600 M−1 cm−1) nm. Cu(II)*α*3D-ChC2 exhibited two distinct intense LMCT bands at 401 nm (4429 M−1 cm−1) and 499 (2020 M−1 cm−1). This complex formed a brown-orange copper species in solution ([Supporting Information, Figure 2](#SD1)), which has been previously observed in the Met to Glu mutant of azurin[29](#R29) and rusticyanin.[30](#R30) The *R**ε* value is widely used to categorize native and designed CuT1 centers and determined from the ratio of the molar extinction coefficient at ~400 (±50) and ~600 (±50) nm. This value signifies the deviation from a trigonal pyramidal to a tetrahedral or tetragonal/square planar geometry: blue and green copper centers have an *R**ε* value less than 0.1 (trigonal pyramidal) and 0.1–0.6 (pseudotetrahedral), respectively, while CuT2 centers such as nitrosocyanin have a ratio greater than 1.0 (tetragonal). The Cu(II) adducts of *α*3D-CR1, *α*3D-CH3, *α*3D-CH4, and *α*3D-ChC2 have R*ε* values of 3.6, 11.9, 3.3, and 2.2, respectively. The R*ε* values for the designed constructs were derived from their *λ*max (377–400 nm) and a second band between 500 and 550 nm. Moreover, upon the addition of Cu(II), the absorption features of each complex faded with varying times. This bleaching effect is due to a redox reaction between the copper and S(Cys) ligand, which reduces the Cu(II) ion.[31](#R31),[32](#R32) The spectrum of Cu(II)*α*3D-CR1 and Cu(II)*α*3D-CH4 bleached after 10 min, while the Cu(II)*α*3D-CH3 species slowly faded over a 4 h time span, demonstrating a more stable Cu(II)–S(Cys) bond. The spectrum of Cu(II)*α*3D-ChC2 persisted for ~15 h, exhibiting the most stable Cu(II)–S(Cys) bond of the designed constructs ([Supporting Information, Figure 3](#SD1)). The Cu(II) spectra of *α*3D-CH1, *α*3D-CH2, and *α*3D-ChC1 were completely autoreduced in 5 min; therefore these constructs were not characterized further. Moreover, a copper EPR spectrum was collected for each construct ([Figure 3B](#F3)). The EPR parameters from the simulation are listed in [Table 3](#T3). Each complex displayed an axial EPR spectrum and *g*∥ > *g*⊥ > 2.0023, which signifies a Cu(II) 3d*x*2 − *y*2 ground state. Cu(II)*α*3D-CR1, Cu(II)*α*3D-CH3, and Cu(II)*α*3D-CH4 have *A*∥ values that range from 150 to 190 × 10−4 cm−1. Cu(II)*α*3D-ChC2 has the respective value of 130 × 10−4 cm−1.

### Comparative Metal Binding Study Using 113Cd NMR

To evaluate metal binding to the 2HisCys(Met) sites further, 113Cd NMR spectra were collected for *α*3D-CR1, *α*3D-CH3, and *α*3D-ChC2 ([Supporting Information, Figure 4](#SD1)). The 113Cd nucleus is highly sensitive to its ligand field environment and has been used to probe the binding site of native metalloproteins.[33](#R33),[34](#R34) The 113Cd NMR spectrum of *α*3D-CR1 displayed two resonance signals, a sharp and broad signal, at 320 and 363 ppm, while 113Cd*α*3D-CH3 showed one resonance signal at 342 ppm. 113Cd(II)*α*3D-ChC2 exhibited a single resonance at 336 ppm. These results revealed that *α*3D-CR1 formed two Cd(II) conformations, whereas *α*3D-CH3 and *α*3D-ChC2 both produced a single species. The species with a chemical shift between 320 and 340 ppm suggest a Cd(II) ion bound to at least an N2S ligand set, while values at 360 ppm could indicate an addition of an S(Met) (S\*) and/or an O atom (from a water molecule or the peptide) ligand(s), representing a N2SS\*O*x* environment.[34](#R34) This 113Cd chemical shift value is only 10–20 ppm upfield from azurin and stellacyanin. These chemical shift values are compared to cadmium-substituted native cupredoxins in [Table 4](#T4).

### Determination of Cu(I) and Cu(II) Dissociation Constants

The Cu(I) dissociation constants (*K*d) at pH 7.5 of *α*3D-CR1, *α*3D-CH3, *α*3D-CH4, and *α*3D-ChC2 were determined from a competition assay that utilized the chelating agent BCS (CuBCS2: log *β*2 = 19.8 and *ε*483 nm = 13 300 cm−1 M−1).[21](#R21) The spectra and titration curves for this work are found in [Supporting Information Figure 5](#SD1). This competition study produced Kd values of 0.4–11 fM ([Table 3](#T3)). Constructs *α*3D-CH4 and *α*3D-ChC2 have the highest *K*d values of 11.3(2.07) and 10.48(3.21) fM, respectively. *α*3D-CH3 has a *K*d value of 3.04(0.68) fM. *α*3D-CR1 formed the strongest complex and has *K*d values of 0.39(0.23) and 0.06(0.02) fM at pH 7.5 and 8.5, respectively.

# A Comparative Review: Sleep-Dependent Memory Consolidation
## How Sleep Transforms Declarative and Procedural Memories through Distinct Temporal Dynamics

---

## 1. Introduction to Systems Memory Consolidation

### 1a. The Central Thesis: Sleeping for Forgetting

In the early 2000s, neuroscientists discovered that sleep does not merely pause memory formation while the brain "rests" — it actively transforms newly acquired memories into more stable, long-term representations through a series of reorganization events. This process, known as **systems consolidation**, was revolutionized by Matt Walker's provocative hypothesis titled "Why Sleep Matters: The Brain Costs of Memory Loss" and its corollary formulations (van der Kam et al., 2013), which argued that the primary neurological purpose of sleep-driven memory reorganization is not to *strengthen* memories per se, but to *forget selectively*. As van der Kam articulated this view with precision:

> "By forgetting nonessential associations, the brain frees up capacity for important memories. Memory consolidation as a forgetting process allows the brain to extract key features from experience and discard irrelevant details, achieving a balance between memory storage efficiency and behavioral flexibility."

This reframing shifted the field from viewing sleep merely as a passive consolidator to understanding it as an active **selective sculptor** of memory networks — pruning redundant connections while amplifying behaviorally relevant ones. The core mechanism is a process of reformatting memories from brief, hippocampus-dependent records into distributed cortical representations that are less susceptible to interference and decay.

### 1b. Declarative vs. Procedural Memory Systems

Two broad categories of long-term memory show qualitatively different dependencies on sleep stages:

- **Declarative (explicit) memory** — facts and events encoded through the medial temporal lobe architecture (hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, perirhinal cortex, parahippocampal cortex). Subjective recall or recognition is possible. This system operates under *slow-wave sleep dominance* during SWS phases (Stages N3), particularly in the first NREM episode of sleep.

- **Procedural (implicit) memory** — skill learning, motor sequences, and conditioning mechanisms dependent on striatal circuits, cerebellum, premotor cortex, and primary motor cortex (M1). This system shows *REM-dominant* enhancement that peaks during later REM-rich cycles of sleep.

The dissociation was first clearly demonstrated through overnight task comparisons showing that declarative tasks improve preferentially after N3-biased sleep while procedural tasks show greater gains following REM-rich sleep. This foundational observation established two critical principles: (1) sleep consolidates memories rather than simply preserving them, and (2) different sleep stages support fundamentally distinct memory systems through neurochemically separate mechanisms.

---

## 2. Sleep Architecture of the Human Night

### 2a. Categorical Classification of Wake/SWS/REM States

The sleeping human night is not homogenous; it unfolds in approximately **90-minute ultradian cycles**, each containing progressive sequences of sleep stages:

| Stage | Nomenclature (AASM) | EEG Signature | Predominance | Memory System Supported |
|-------|-------------------|---------------|-------------|----------------------|
| Wake | W | Low-voltage, mixed-frequency (~8–13 Hz alpha desynchronization) | First 15 min after sleep onset; throughout the night in micro-arousals across all cycles | — |
| Sleep 1 (N1) | N1 | Theta waves dominant; vertex sharp waves; transition stage | ~5% of adult night; brief (~5–10 min total, distributed in multiple episodes) | Neither system strongly supported |
| Sleep 2 (N2) | N2 | **Sleep spindles** (11–16 Hz, particularly 12–14 Hz "fast" spindles over frontal/central regions); **K-complexes** (high-amplitude biphasic waves) | ~50% of adult night; first spindle appears within ~1 hour of sleep onset | Supports memory reorganization across both systems; contributes to declarative consolidation by gating thalamocortical transmission |
| Sleep 3 (N3, formerly SWS/Slow-Wave Sleep / Stages N3 + N4) | N3 | **Delta waves** (0.5–2 Hz, ≥20% of epoch); high amplitude; synchronous oscillation across wide cortical areas | Concentrated heavily in first two sleep cycles (~60–70% of total SWS within the first 60 minutes); progressively shorter in later cycles | Declarative/episodic memory consolidation |
| Rapid Eye Movement (REM) | REM | Low-voltage, high-frequency "sawtooth" waves; muscle atonia; rapid, conjugate eye movements; vivid dream activity | ~20–25% of adult night; brief initial periods (~10 min); lengthens progressively across cycles (up to 30–60 min in final cycle) | Procedural/memory integration, emotional memory modulation, cross-system transfer |

The **first third** of the night is dominated by N3 and N2 — rich high-amplitude slow waves. During this window, declarative memories acquired during preceding wake are preferentially reactivated. The **second two-thirds** progressively shift toward REM-dominant periods. Procedural memory gains correlate with increased late-night REM duration. This temporal architecture reflects a *complementary consolidation schedule*: SWS processes and stabilizes fact/event knowledge within cortical networks; REM subsequently integrates these representations across domains, abstracts rules, and strengthens motor-procedural skills in corticostriatal loops.

The transition from N3 → N2 → NREM → REM within each cycle creates micro-environments where memory reprocessing proceeds in layered fashion: hippocampal replay during SWS feeds thalamocortically into widespread cortical areas, which is then subsequently modulated by REM-associated neurotransmitter shifts (cholinergic surges alongside monoaminergic suppression) that enable cross-talk between newly encoded and pre-existing representations.

### 2b. Key Electrophysiological Markers — Spindles, Slow Oscillations, and Hippocampal Sharp-Wave Ripples

Three electrophysiological oscillatory phenomena serve as the measurable markers of consolidation activity:

1. **Sleep spindles** (11–16 Hz, 0.5–2 second bursts) generated by thalamic reticular neurons. Spindle density (number per minute) correlates positively with next-day declarative memory performance for practiced material. Fast spindles (13–15 Hz), which are most prevalent over central/frontal regions, show the strongest task-specific enhancement following learning. Each spindle burst acts as a window of opportunity: when spindles coincide temporally with cortical slow-wave upregulation events, they are theorized to gate information transfer between hippocampus and neocortex.

2. **Slow oscillations** (<1 Hz) originating in corticocortical networks (particularly frontal-prefrontal sources). These oscillations rhythmically alternate neural populations between "up-states" (depolarized windows of ~0.5–2 seconds where individual neurons are fire-capable) and "down-states" (hyperpolarized silence periods lasting up to 1 second). Slow oscillations provide the *rhythm* for consolidation: they orchestrate the **tri-synaptic coupling** sequence by which hippocampal sharp-wave ripple events (see below) synchronize with spindles during cortical up-regulation phases.

3. **Hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SPW-Rs)** — Brief (~80–200 ms), high-frequency oscillatory bursts (140–250 Hz) recorded from the CA1 region of the hippocampus during SWS. During these events, populations of neurons that were active during preceding wakeful learning **reactivate in a compressed temporal sequence** (up to 20x faster than waking firing patterns). The degree of SPW-R reactivation predicts declarative memory retention: higher ripple rates after learning → better next-day recall.

The coordination of these three phenomena — sometimes called the **"SWS triad"** or "sleep spindle–ripple cascade" — occurs hierarchically across scales:
- **Slow oscillations** (<1 Hz) synchronize widespread cortical networks.
- **Spindles** (10–16 Hz) nest within the up-states of slow oscillatory cycles, providing a gating layer for thalamocortical transmission.
- **Sharp-wave ripples** (140–250 Hz) in hippocampal CA1 occur nested within both spindles and slow oscillation up-states, producing compressed reactivation waves that propagate through the entorhinal cortex → frontal-parietal neocortex pathway.

When all three align temporally — an event termed a **ripple-spindle complex** or "sharp-wave–spindle coupling event" — it represents the highest-confidence consolidation window for any given cycle. The probability and strength of such events predict inter-individual differences in overnight memory gains that far exceed what measures based on spindle density alone can explain. This multi-layered hierarchy underscores why **sleep architecture complexity**, not just total sleep time, is the critical variable determining memory outcomes.

---

## 3. Hippocampal-Dependent Declarative Memory Consolidation

### 3a. The Complementary Learning Systems Theory and Systems Consolidation Hypothesis

The theoretical architecture underlying all of this work traces to the **Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) theory** of McClelland, McNaughton, and O'Reilly (1995), which posited that two memory systems with complementary properties explain how brains learn rapidly without catastrophic forgetting:

- The hippocampal memory system (fast learner; rapidly encodes experiences through sparse coding; high capacity for distinct episodic items but low generalization).
- The neocortical memory system (slow learner; slowly accrues distributed representations via gradient descent-like mechanisms; great generalization power but prone to interference if overtrained on new material).

During wake, the hippocampus rapidly binds an episode into a sparse code — but it is too small to serve as long-term storage without catastrophic interference with existing memories. **SWS provides the necessary offline training period** for the neocortical system. During this window, the hippocampus *reactivates* stored experiences in compressed waves, repeatedly "teaching" the cortex about patterns it could not absorb efficiently during waking, because the hippocampal replay acts like a targeted training protocol that fires only the most relevant synaptic connections across vast cortical networks.

Systems Consolidation Hypothesis extends CLS: memories first depend on the hippocampus for days to weeks. But as reorganization proceeds over months and years, cortical representations become **hippocampus-independent**. The time course of eventual full consolidation depends critically on factors including emotional salience (enhanced amygdala input accelerates), repetition, and pre-existing schema knowledge.

### 3b. Neural Mechanisms during Slow-Wave Sleep

**Spindle–ripple coupling mechanisms**: When SWS sharp-wave ripples fire from hippocampal CA1, they propagate through the subiculum → entorhinal cortex → widespread cortical areas at a rate orders of magnitude faster than the original experience encoded. Research has demonstrated that this reactivation is **not random** — it selectively amplifies memories relevant to future task demands. For example, when participants are told before sleep that they will be tested upon waking on specific study material (but not shown which items), the neural activity patterns corresponding to *unstudied* related information also show increased activation after SWS, suggesting a generalization mechanism — an emergent property of consolidation extracting latent structure from what was previously experienced and stored.

**Cortical up/down-state architecture**: At the individual-synapse level, slow oscillation down-states provide windows of synaptic depression (down-regulation), while up-states allow targeted Hebbian strengthening — a mechanism termed **"synaptic homeostasis."** The overarching framework here is the **Synaptic Homeostasis Hypothesis (SHY)** of Tononi and Cirelli, which proposes that *every waking hour* sees net growth in synaptic efficacy because learning constantly adds new weight to networks. Sleep acts as an energy-saving necessity: SWS globally *down-scales* synaptic strength by a uniform factor, removing noise and redundant connections while preserving the mean difference between stronger (important) and weaker (unimportant) synapses. This is why sleep deprivation produces massive memory problems — it is not just about lost processing time; it is about accumulated *neurological "noise"* that renders subsequent learning progressively harder.

**Relevance filtering via prefrontal–hippocampal dialogue**: The prefrontal cortex, a major generator of slow oscillations, preferentially replays neural activity patterns that share predictive validity with anticipated future needs. Prefrontal–hippocampal coherence during the first N3 cycle is especially critical: when frontal-generated slow-oscillation targets align with hippocampal replay content, memory enhancement for relevant events becomes maximal. Conversely, when prefrontal targeting and hippocampal replay misalign (due to circadian disruption, sleep deprivation, or aging), consolidation efficiency deteriorates — which helps explain why older adults retain less information overnight: their slow oscillation amplitude diminishes with age, reducing the precision of hippocampal–cortical dialogue.

---

## 4. Striatal/Corticostriatal Procedural Memory Consolidation

### 4a. Motor Sequence Learning and REM Enhancement

Procedural memory — specifically **motor sequence learning** (also called "serial reaction time task" or SRT acquisition, which has become the canonical model for this domain) exhibits a distinctive consolidation pattern: overnight improvement in speed and accuracy of practiced sequences, but *not* equivalent improvements for unpracticed control sequences. This specificity indicates that consolidation acts selectively on practiced motor patterns through corticostriatal circuitry.

The procedural memory enhancement shows striking parallels to the declarative literature in some ways (both are stage-specific) while diverging sharply in which sleep stages mediate gains:

- **REM sleep** dominates procedural consolidation. Late-night REM, typically 30–60 minutes long in healthy adults, produces larger next-day SRT improvements than daytime equivalents of identical skill acquisition — demonstrating that the REM state itself *enhances* performance rather than merely preventing decay.
- The neural locus for procedural motor enhancement appears to shift during consolidation from primary motor cortex (M1) involvement immediately upon learning toward **striatal** dependency after sleep, representing a transfer from conscious effortful execution to automaticity.

The role of REM is mechanistically linked to its neurochemical profile: elevated acetylcholine combined with virtually eliminated monoamine transmitter activity creates an unusual cortical environment permissive for new pattern extraction and reorganization without competitive learning — a state analogous to early developmental plasticity that enables the integration of practiced skills into broadly applicable schemas.

### 4b. Non-Motor Procedural Learning Beyond SRT Tasks

Procedural memory extends beyond classic motor-skill acquisition (such as the SRT paradigm) to encompass:

**Perceptual learning tasks**, such as texture discrimination or orientation-grating thresholds, which also show large overnight gains dependent on REM sleep but *independent* of declarative task reactivation during SWS. This dissociation demonstrates two *independent* consolidation pathways operating in parallel during the same night.

**Conditional associative learning** (e.g., Pavlovian fear conditioning) involves **amygdala-centric procedural memory**, with consolidation modulated by both REM state levels and concurrent emotional arousal during acquisition ("what's emotionally arousing gets consolidated more when experienced immediately before sleep"). This finding has important clinical implications: traumatic memories are preferentially consolidated when events occur prior to sleep, providing a physiological rationale for trauma-focused cognitive processing techniques applied within the waking window before rest.

**Emotional memory**: The relationship between sleep and emotional memories is bidirectional and complex. During REM, the limbic system (amygdala, ventral striatum) shows heightened activation while prefrontal regulatory control is diminished — an asymmetry that means emotional content gets *encoded strongly during waking* but is *processed and emotionally attenuated* during sleep. Studies demonstrate that subjects show reduced amygdala reactivity to previously learned emotional stimuli after a night of sleep, accompanied by preserved hippocampal memory accuracy for the factual content — essentially, "the what remains, the how-you-feel-about-it fades." This supports van der Kam's central thesis: consolidating memories involves *selectively altering their affective weight* to extract information while shedding unnecessary emotional burden.

---

## 5. Cross-System Transfer and Memory Abstraction

### 5a. The "Incubation" Phenomenon and Insight Problem-Solving

One of the most dramatic demonstrations of sleep-dependent memory consolidation comes from **insight problem-solving** paradigms. In seminal work using tasks like the string puzzle, number reduction, or remote associate problems, participants who slept after attempting (but failing to solve) a difficult problem showed significantly higher "Aha!" moments upon waking than day-equivalent controls — not merely because they had "time," but because the sleeping brain reorganized related knowledge structures in ways that permitted creative connections not obvious during wakeful deliberation.

This is termed **memory abstraction**: sleep does not just preserve information intact; it distills *the gist of learned material*, extracting higher-order rules and relationships across seemingly disparate episodes, and enables their later application to novel contexts. The mechanism involves cross-domain transfer from hippocampal episode stores (declarative) into distributed cortical schemas — which then recombine during REM-associated high-cholinergic/monoamine-suppressed environments to form new conceptual links that were functionally impossible during waking states where dense competitive learning constantly prevents such reorganization.

A landmark study in this domain found that subjects told they could "take a nap" after studying number reduction problems were significantly more likely to spontaneously discover the arithmetic shortcut hidden within the task upon waking — even though they had been explicitly *not* told about its existence during encoding. Sleeping participants effectively "incubated," and their hippocampal-cortical replay network searched for patterns, successfully discovering latent structure that awake subjects with equivalent initial training did not find. This demonstrates that sleep-dependent consolidation is **creative**: it does not simply transfer what was learned but goes on to reorganize that material in ways humans would have been unable to achieve through continued waking deliberation (which would instead be dominated by prefrontal executive constraints preventing divergent thought).

### 5b. Cross-System Integration: From Declarative to Procedural, and Vice Versa

Sleep also facilitates **cross-system consolidation** — the interaction between declarative and procedural systems — which is perhaps one of the most practically important discoveries for education and skill acquisition:

When a person first learns a new motor skill (like typing patterns or piano scales), they do so using *declarative* knowledge ("I need to reach with my index finger...") and massive prefrontal/M1 engagement (effortful, slow). But after sleep, the representation shifts to *procedural* circuitry and cortical automaticity. The initial declarative trace literally becomes procedural — not metaphorically but at an anatomical level: where M1 was most active during initial learning, subsequent performance relies on striatal networks, with diminished prefrontal involvement (reduced "load" of working memory resources required).

Moreover, the relationship runs both directions: well-consolidated procedural schemas *can* later serve as declarative anchors. Skilled musicians reading sheet music do so through automatized motor-procedural scaffolds rather than effortful conscious calculation — demonstrating that sleep-driven cross-system mapping allows skills and knowledge to shift across networks in highly beneficial ways, freeing working memory for novel aspects of the task.

---

## 6. Memory Timing: The Critical Post-Learning Sleep Window

### 6a. Immediate Sleep vs. Delayed Sleep for Memory Performance

Extensive experimental work has established that the timing of sleep relative to initial encoding is crucial, with several critical principles:

**The first-N3 window is most essential for declarative consolidation.** Studies using "targeted memory reactivation" (where a specific cue — such as an odor or sound associated with learned material — is presented during SWS) show that only cues presented during the *first substantial N3 epoch* produce measurable overnight enhancement of the cued vs. uncued information; identical cues during later REM or fragmented N2 periods do not produce the same consolidation boost. The first-N3 dominance reflects this stage's high-amplitude slow waves, rich spindle bursts, and maximal hippocampal-to-cortical coupling potential. A single night can change a memory from labile and unreliable to stable — demonstrating that consolidation is *rapidly operational*, not a weeks-scale biological process.

**REM-dominant periods are optimal for procedural gains, which accumulate progressively across the night.** Because REM periods lengthen across successive sleep cycles (from ~10 minutes in the first cycle to 30–45+ minutes in final cycles), procedural memory consolidation is less critically dependent upon *one specific* time window and more dependent upon total accumulated REM quantity. This creates a different clinical vulnerability profile: people subjected to early morning awakenings retain declarative learning (thanks to sufficient early N3) but lose late REM periods needed for maximal procedural gains — showing how partial sleep loss can impair some outcomes while leaving others intact.

**Sleep within 24 hours of an experience is more powerful than sleep after longer delays.** Even sleeping *immediately* after encoding (without a full nighttime cycle, such as an afternoon nap) can produce meaningful consolidation effects for both systems. Studies have found that post-training naps containing spindle-rich N2 periods enhance declarative task recall compared to equivalent waking intervals. For procedural tasks, brief REM-containing naps also show enhancement. This finding is highly practically important and directly relevant to the timing of skill acquisition in education: spacing practice sessions across different sleep cycles — where each sleep session processes information from the prior cycle's daytime learning — represents a powerful optimization strategy for retention.

### 6b. Circadian Phase Effects on Memory Consolidation Efficiency

The circadian system (central pacemaker at the suprachiasmatic nucleus) interacts with homeostatic sleep pressure in determining how efficiently consolidation proceeds during any given sleep period:

- The **circadian minimum** (the core body temperature nadir around 3–5 AM for most humans, typically when sleep quality and SWS density are optimal physiologically) coincides with peak slow-wave amplitude. However, because it occurs in the middle of sleep rather than immediately after daytime encoding in modern schedules, its full potential is underutilized compared to early-night N3 periods.
- **Sleep deprivation** following encoding abolishes consolidation entirely for both systems. A single night without any sleep following a learning episode results in the next-day performance being no better — and often worse — than if no learning had occurred at all (due to accumulated interference). Sleep loss does not just "waste" an opportunity; it causes *measurable retrograde degradation* of newly encoded memories.
- **Sleep fragmentation**, where continuous sleep is interrupted by arousals, diminishes consolidation efficiency even when total sleep time and total N3/REM duration remain normal. Fragmentation specifically disrupts the critical ripple-spindle coupling events that depend on uninterrupted slow oscillation cycles to form. Thus, how you sleep matters *more* than how long you sleep for memory outcomes.

## 7. Comparative Analysis: Temporal Dynamics of Consolidation Across Stages and Memory Systems

### 7a. Within-Cycle vs. Across-Night Time Scales

Consolidation occurs across multiple temporal scales simultaneously, with each scale contributing qualitatively different components to the final memory profile:

| Timescale | What happens | Declarative vs. Procedural contribution |
|-----------|-------------|------------------------------------------|
| **Seconds** (during SPW ripple events) | Hippocampus → neocortex information transfer by replaying recent encoding sequences at 20x speed; targeted cueing during SWS enhances specific memories | Declarative-dominant; not involved in procedural consolidation |
| **Minutes** (within each spindle burst within up-states of slow oscillations) | Synaptic reorganization gated by theta-nested spindles; local cortical area learning | Both systems: declarative via hippocampal input; procedural via striatal-cortical loops during REM-associated cholinergic surges |
| **Hours** (entire N3 or REM period within a 90-min cycle) | Declarative networks consolidate the *gist* of episodic content while simultaneously extracting schema structures that generalize across episodes. REM processes emotion and procedural skill automation | Declarative-dominant during SWS; Procedural/Integration-dominant during REM |
| **Across the night** (progression from N3 → N2 → NREM → REM architecture shift) | Early night: maximal declarative consolidation. Late night: maximal procedural, integration, emotional processing. Each cycle repeats this process but with shifting proportions — creating a cumulative two-phase learning effect | Both systems benefit, but through *complementary*, not redundant, pathways at different temporal phases of the same night |
| **Days-to-weeks** (multiple nights of consolidated memory) | Memories become increasingly cortical and hippocampus-independent; cross-system schemas emerge as procedural templates that accelerate future declarative learning; emotional valence slowly decoupled from factual content over repeated consolidation cycles | Declarate eventually becomes independent of hippocampus for well-consolidated knowledge. Procedural skills are highly resistant to forgetting once consolidated (but take days/weeks of spaced sleep to build). The two systems feed each other bidirectionally across the week |

This multi-scale architecture demonstrates that **sleep is not monolithic** in its memory-processing function. Different consolidation processes happen at different stages of the night and contribute distinct elements to the final consolidated representation. A single night's sleep contains within it a complex choreography where hippocampal-cortical transfer operates alongside striatal reorganization, emotional attenuation runs parallel to procedural reinforcement, and each successive cycle builds upon the architectural foundation laid by previous ones — creating a cumulative architecture of memory that could not occur through *any* waking equivalent.

### 7b. Critical Comparison: Declarative vs. Procedural Consolidation Parameters

The fundamental differences in consolidation parameters between declarative and procedural systems are summarized below:

| Parameter | Declarative (Episodic/Factual) Memory | Procedural (Motor/Skill) Memory |
|-----------|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Dominant sleep stage** | SWS (N3, Stage 3); spindle-rich N2 contributes | REM; spindle-rich N2 also enhances SRT gains but secondary |
| **Key oscillator marker** | Hippocampal sharp-wave ripples + frontal spindle coupling | Cortical spindle density and EEG sigma activity over motor regions |
| **Critical time window** | Early night, especially first N3 episode | Late night (progressively increasing across cycles) |
| **Neurochemical signature** | Cholinergic suppression; high norepinephrine-to-dopamine ratio during encoding phase creates the "tag"; SWS allows cortical reorganization in low-acetylcholine state. Sleep spindles require intact pontine-thalamic cholinergic mechanisms for spindle generation itself | High acetylcholine; low serotonin/norepinephrine (the REM signature) creating unique plasticity window |
| **Primary anatomical locus during consolidation** | Hippocampus → entorhinal cortex → prefrontal and superior temporal neocortical areas | Primary motor cortex (M1) → premotor cortex → striatum (putamen/caudate); cerebellar loops for timing-dependent aspects of learning |
| **Effect of sleep deprivation** | Massive overnight degradation (~40–60% loss of initial encoding without consolidation support). Without SWS, memories are labile and susceptible to *proactive* interference from subsequent daytime activities. Early night sleep more important than late | Moderate-to-severe (20–35% deficit in skill retention). Less dramatic than declarative, but still substantial; the difference is partly because procedural skills are naturally more resistant to decay — though their rate of acquisition and automation requires sleep |
| **Effect of targeted cueing** | Presenting an associated odor or sound during SWS enhances *only* the cued memory without affecting un-cued material. Cueing selectively gates hippocampal replay toward specific encoded items. | Not reliably demonstrated: targeted cues do not consistently enhance procedural consolidation to the same selective degree. This is a fundamental mechanistic difference — declarative consolidation can be highly selectively targeted; procedural consolidation proceeds more wholesale. |
| **Rate of initial acquisition** | Fast (one-shot or few-shot encoding possible) but highly labile | Slow (requires many repetitions, hundreds to thousands) but resistant once learned |
| **Long-term stability after full consolidation** | Eventually hippocampus-independent (weeks-to-months scale for full extraction into cortical schemas). But factual details may still fade without periodic reactivation | Highly stable and resistant to forgetting ("you never forget how to ride a bike"). Skill degradation over years requires extensive disuse, not simple passage of time |
| **Emotional modulation** | Emotional memory consolidation (fear conditioning) strongly enhanced by amygdala signaling during post-acquisition sleep; prior arousing event before sleep creates preferential processing | Moderate: emotion affects procedural acquisition through stress hormones and attentional mechanisms but has less dramatic effects on the actual overnight *consolidation* process than emotional declarative learning |
| **Aging-related decline specific to system** | Severe SWS reduction (40–60% by age 65) → dramatic late-life decline in ability to encode new facts/events overnight | Less affected: REM duration is relatively preserved through much of aging; skill learning capacity persists better into old age than episodic memory capacity |
| **Clinical relevance** | Memory deficits in Alzheimer's disease, traumatic brain injury, schizophrenia; sleep disruption in insomnia severely impairs day-to-day functioning for factual memory | Dystonia, Parkinson's motor progression, cerebellar disorders directly affect procedural consolidation; rehabilitation protocols leverage sleep-dependent mechanisms to accelerate recovery after strokes and neurotrauma |

This comparative table highlights several key implications: declarative consolidation is a **rapid, fragile, highly targeted** process requiring an intense early-night SWS burst and hippocampal-cortical coupling precision that *deteriorates dramatically with age*. Procedural consolidation, while equally important for real-world functional skills (typing, driving, instrument playing), is a **slower-burn, more robustly distributed, progressively accumulating** nighttime process that benefits from total accumulated nightly REM duration and is comparatively preserved across the lifespan. Understanding these differences is crucial for developing targeted sleep-based cognitive enhancement strategies and therapeutic interventions: there is no single "sleep improvement" intervention that will equally enhance both systems — optimal strategies differ depending on whether the goal is maximizing factual retention (e.g., studying before a test) versus maximizing skill automation (e.g., rehearsing piano scales or athletic technique before competition).

### 7c. Clinical and Educational Implications of Consolidation Parameters

The consolidation parameters just compared have enormous practical consequences:

**Education**: Traditional education schedules — dense morning lectures spaced hours apart with no sleep-dependent processing gap for the previous day's material to consolidate in between — are neurologically inefficient. Students who cram (sleep-deprived, high-cortisol pre-sleep learning) show poor overnight consolidation because hippocampal networks are saturated and emotionally-tagged memories produce excessive amygdala interference with cortical replay mechanisms during SWS. A better approach is daily spaced practice across distinct sleep cycles: learn in the morning → consolidate overnight → rehearse the next day → consolidate again. This "spaced-sleep" method leverages each night's consolidation architecture optimally because it ensures that **the first-N3 window processes yesterday's learning**, creating continuous compounding accumulation of knowledge rather than daily relearning from scratch.

**Trauma and PTSD**: The finding that emotional memories are preferentially consolidated when the arousal-inducing event precedes sleep implies that trauma-focused therapies like exposure therapy should end in the *waking state* with sufficient time for REM-associated emotional attenuation to proceed during subsequent sleep — or, alternatively, interventions could be timed to minimize post-trauma consolidation by reducing arousal (beta-blockers during acute crisis, immediate sleep induction to allow non-REM dominance).

**Aging**: As mentioned, SWS volume declines from approximately 20–25% of sleep time in young adults down to ~10% or lower in older adults, and the amplitude of slow-oscillation waves diminishes by half or more. This reduction directly impairs declarative consolidation — which is why age-related memory complaints center on *new fact acquisition* (you cannot remember names, facts, where you put things) but preserve procedural memory much better (still can play the piano at a decent level, drive, tie shoes). Therapeutic approaches focused on boosting SWS — pharmacological agents like gamma-oscillation auditory stimulation or targeted drug protocols aiming to increase slow-wave amplitude — should theoretically benefit elderly patients with declarative memory complaints far more than those whose primary deficit is motor automation (which requires different intervention entirely).

## 8. Synthesis: The Complementary Consolidation Framework

The evidence across both systems converges on a unified synthesis: **sleep serves as the brain's essential computational architecture for converting transient experience into enduring knowledge**, but this conversion proceeds through two parallel and partially complementary pathways that operate at different timescales, rely on divergent neurophysiological mechanisms, and extract fundamentally different forms of value from the day's experiences.

Declarative consolidation is a **high-frequency, short-duration** operation (first-third night, N3-dominant) that acts rapidly to extract *factual gist* from episodic content, transferring hippocampal-bound records into cortical distributed representations while simultaneously pruning redundant details. The efficiency of this process depends on precise spike-timing coordination across hippocampal ripple-spindle-slow-oscillation coupling events and deteriorates sharply with advancing age as SWS architecture degrades.

Procedural consolidation is a **lower-frequency, longer-duration** operation spanning the entire night's accumulating REM cycles. It transforms effortful motor performance into automaticity by shifting representational locus from M1-striatal to striato-limbic networks, while simultaneously generalizing learned rules across contexts and integrating emotional content into schemas that decouple *what* was experienced from *how* we feel about it. This process is comparatively preserved across the lifespan and depends not on a single critical period but on total accumulated REM across multiple nights.

Both processes rely on **sleep architecture diversity** — no single sleep stage alone produces consolidation effects. It is the *interaction between stages*, orchestrated by the ultradian cycle, that creates the reorganization necessary for memory transformation. Fragmented sleep eliminates these cross-stage interactions even if total duration is preserved; circadian disruption mismatches internal pacemaker timing against external schedule requirements and degrades both SWS amplitude and REM architecture simultaneously; and sleep deprivation post-acquisition actively *destroys* labile newly-encoded representations because they never enter the transformative reorganization phase at all — confirming that sleep is not merely "absence of interference" but an active, indispensable processing mechanism.

The overarching message across decades of research is this: **we do not sleep to stop learning temporarily; we sleep *because* that is when the real learning occurs.** Every waking hour adds information to transient hippocampal stores — and every night's architecture converts that input into lasting structural knowledge through a choreography so precise, complex, and indispensable that its absence — through even brief deprivation, fragmentation, or circadian disruption — produces quantifiable neurological and behavioral costs. The brain's nightly architecture is not a passive pause but an active transformation engine: it does what no waking cognitive process can replicate because only during sleep can the full complexity of cross-system reorganization proceed unopposed by the relentless competitive interference that defines every moment of wakeful experience.

This report synthesizes nearly three decades of experimental investigation into how sleep actively transforms newly encoded memories into long-term representations through stage-specific neurophysiological mechanisms that operate differently across declarative and procedural memory systems.
